Article Title: Darren Caldeira: 'OCI players are a quick fix; grassroots must remain the priority'
Article Text:
Bengaluru FC's Director of Football Darren Caldeira (R) with a player. (Photo by special arrangement)

NEW DELHI:

EXCERPTS

Q. The ISL is entering its first season under a club-led model. What do you make of it, and why did we reach such a stage?

Darren Caldeira:

Bengaluru FC Director of Football Darren Caldeira. (Photo by special arrangement)

Q. From an organisational perspective, how do things change for clubs under this model?

Caldeira:

We haven't signed any domestic players this season. But there's a reason for that because we've got a very strong, robust youth academy that is churning out players year on year. We've had a couple of them make their debuts last season. Darren Caldeira | Bengaluru FC's Director of Football

Q. Has that uncertainty changed the way Bengaluru FC have approached transfers and squad building?

Darren Caldeira:

We are a club that's very, very focused on that academy and we don't need to go and sign players from the outset. So even if tomorrow, we feel we've lost a quality player, maybe an Ashique (Kuruniyan) or maybe a Ryan (Williams) or someone. We know that we've got a replacement within the academy. Darren Caldeira | Bengaluru FC's Director of Football

Q. Is Bengaluru FC's academy-first approach the model Indian football should be following?

Darren Caldeira:

Q. Should the ISL introduce salary caps?

Darren Caldeira:

Ryan Williams gave up his Australian passport to play for India.(Instagram)

Q. Where do you stand on the idea of

OCI players

in the ISL?

Darren Caldeira:

Indian football as a whole, we can do everything we can at the club level and the league level, but it's really important that the national team does well. So every competition that they are participating in, whether it's your SAFF Cup or whether it's these friendlies that are coming now (against Panama, Brazil and Uruguay), good performances at the international level do help us because there are a lot of eyeballs. Darren Caldeira | Bengaluru FC's Director of Football

Q. What would success look like for the new ISL, for Bengaluru FC, and for Indian football?

Darren Caldeira:

Indian football enters a new era in the upcoming season with the Indian Super League (ISL) transitioning to a club-led model, placing greater responsibility on clubs to shape the league's commercial and sporting future. For Bengaluru FC , that means balancing ambition with sustainability while adapting to a fundamentally different operating landscape.In an exclusive conversation with TimesofIndia.com, Bengaluru FC's Director of Football Darren Caldeira speaks about the opportunities and challenges of the new ISL, the club's academy-driven recruitment strategy, the case for salary limits, the debate around Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) players, and why he believes long-term investment in youth — not quick fixes — will determine Indian football's future.I think it's a positive step in my opinion. If you look at it globally as well, it's not like this is a new phenomenon put together. It's not always that you have the federations running the leagues or somebody else coming in, like a commercial partner, like we had before (Football Sports Development Limited), running the league.So I think this club-led model, there's air of optimism from a lot of the conversations we are having, as well that probably this could be the right way forward. And while I say that, I don't want to sugarcoat things. There are still a lot of formalities that need to be closed.But I genuinely believe that we are heading in the right direction through a lot of these offline conversations, whether it's sponsorship or production, I will have to give credit to the FSDL as well in terms of a lot of the good work they've done. Because now that we are getting our hands dirty, actually being the ones that are having these conversations, whether it's broadcasters, whether it's sponsorship, you just realise there's so many things to cover. But then again, we've taken it up as a challenge.We're slowly onboarding a central team that comes in and we've already kind of had some soft integrations. But in my opinion, I think we are heading in the right direction.I think, more than anything, the whole commercial risk sits with the clubs, right? We are the ones having these hard conversations. Previously, it was FSDL speaking with production houses and broadcasters. We knew that we would be playing the league after paying X amount in terms of the franchise fee, and at the end of the year, there would be some sort of central revenue coming in. So that was a given.It was easier for clubs to plan as well because you knew what it would look like. Right now, there is that little bit of uncertainty that we talk about. You still don't know what the numbers would look like or what the Profit & Loss (P&L) would look like.We've got tentative numbers that we've put down, but a lot of owners are still a little more cautious, while also being excited about how we can take control of things, probably bring down costs in certain verticals and focus on the marketing of the league.So, more than anything, I would say the commercial risk is a big change.There are two things to that. We are a football club that has always been challenging for the ISL Shield or the title. We always want to win, right? But we are also mindful of the fact that the club economics have changed, and Indian football economics have changed.That said, we haven't signed any domestic players this season. But there's a reason for that because we've got a very strong, robust youth academy that is churning out players year on year. We've had a couple of them make their debuts last season.This time around, we didn't extend the contracts of four or five players. Some of them are leaders in the group as well. But we felt we had good replacements coming in from our B team to the first team.So the focus was on how we could probably get some good, solid foreign players in. Last season, we only had two foreigners in our squad, and we missed out on the title by three points.So you never know, if we had two or three more foreigners, we could have been a lot more competitive, probably taking it down to the wire. The focus was more on foreign players this time around because we knew we had the Indian contingent pretty much sorted.The idea was to get certain profiles that we felt would strengthen the team. There was a lot of work involved with Pep [Muñoz] and me to make sure we got the players who would enhance what we already had and would be essential to pushing towards the league Shield.We've always been a football club (that is) big on the academy. You look at our first team right now, we've got more than half of the squad that have been part of our academy.And for us, it's a no-brainer. A lot of teams, when they had to strengthen their squads in the summer, had to reach out to other clubs, look at the free agents and things like that. And all we had to do was look right into our academy straight away to see who comes in.So for us, we're always looking to get those right players in because like I said, the economics of the league has changed as well. There's been this constant conversation about probably Indian players' salaries being inflated. I think that bubble has burst to a certain extent.But then again, we are a club that's very, very focused on that academy and we don't need to go and sign players from the outset. So even if tomorrow, we feel we've lost a quality player, maybe an Ashique (Kuruniyan) or maybe a Ryan (Williams) or someone. We know that we've got a replacement within the academy.Of course, we'll probably not be at that level and cannot hit the ground running, but we're ready to throw them in the deep end. I think Pep's also very big on age is not a factor. Nationality is not a factor to us. If you're good enough, you're old enough.100 percent. We've had these conversations internally as well, and a lot of clubs have spoken about it. I think it's more about the clubs coming forward and saying, "Listen, this is the number, whatever that number is, and let's all stay within that."I think we've had salary caps in previous seasons as well. It's not like this is a new conversation we're having. I won't get into the details of whether people are following the salary caps or not, but there are always loopholes with any system.So I think the best way forward is for clubs to figure out how we fix this issue around salaries. The clubs are taking a step forward and coming together, saying, "Listen, we need to keep it within these numbers."We know that some of us have longer contracts with certain players, and you can't change those numbers now. But I think that conversation has already started, and we've already started making changes.While we're doing that, we're also figuring out a mechanism that can work because it's easier said than done. How do you have a bulletproof auditing system? It's not the MLS, where contracts are centralised and the league controls the contracts. Here, every club controls its own contracts.But, like I said, I think the clubs are making an effort, and that's a good sign.So for me, when you talk about OCI players, I remember when that conversation started a couple of months ago, just like probably any other club, there were quite a few agents and the OCI players that reached out directly in terms of we are available, we are ready to come and we want to be part of the system.But I don't think it was well thought through. In my opinion, it was more about, there was a lot of public speaking about it, a lot of social media attention. But are these players wanting to come to Indian football for the right reasons? Will they actually come and spend those 2-3 years in Indian football, work on their paperwork and actually surrender their passport if they have to take that Indian passport?Something that I'd also like to mention is that sometimes when we think of OCI players and we think of foreign players, we already think of these players are better than our players, and that's not the case.Of course, there are a few who are playing at a certain level and will come in and change the whole dynamics of the Indian national team if that matters. But there are also a lot of players who are playing in Europe, but I wouldn't say are better than our Indian boys right now. So even if we have to go ahead with this, we need to be sure that we have a list of say 10-15 quality players from certain areas around the world, and these are the guys we want to get in.But more than anything, I think this is temporary. It's a quick fix. I think the focus should always be focussing on grassroots and the youth academy. And I think if all the stakeholders, everybody comes together, I think that should be the primary focus.I think, for starters, just going back to the home-and-away format and having a full-fledged season would be a good starting point. It's not a truncated format. We're going back to home-and-away, and we're having playoffs again. I really do wish we had another 30 or 60 days because we are having a lot of really good conversations, but it's so time-sensitive that you can't implement certain things that we want to.But whether it's your broadcasters, sponsorship, or an international partner wanting to come in, if we had that little bit of runway, I think it would be a lot better. But having a full-fledged season is one thing.It's just going back to what the ISL would look like and then gradually getting the right partners in, whether it's your sponsors. It could be as simple as your kit partners or your ball partners. But we're having a lot of encouraging conversations. While there is a lot of negativity surrounding Indian football, I won't deny that. There is still this air of optimism with the clubs kind of driving it and what Indian football looks like.At the club level, of course, it's Pep getting his first full season. I would love for him to be successful because he's a pretty solid coach. He brought a good bunch of players who have come in as well. And with our academy, it's about keeping the players coming through.And our soccer school, which I talk about as well, is more like a sort of business, and that does well as well. So overall, just for all of that, for the club to run smoothly, we move towards a sustainable model and we win trophies. And that's what I would see from a BFC level.And Indian football as a whole, we can do everything we can at the club level and the league level, but it's really important that the national team does well. So every competition that they are participating in, whether it's your SAFF Cup or whether it's these friendlies that are coming now (against Panama, Brazil and Uruguay), good performances at the international level do help us because there are a lot of eyeballs. People are watching from the outside, and the national team and the league go kind of hand in hand. So, hoping for some positive results there.
Article Summary: Bengaluru FC's Director of Football Darren Caldeira speaks to TimesofIndia.com about the new ISL, the club's academy-driven recruitment strategy, and the case for salary limits. He also discusses the debate around Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) players.

Article Title: Bronze for Anant Jeet Naruka, Parinaaz Dhaliwal in Asian Games 2026 mixed skeet
Article Text:
India's Parinaaz Dhaliwal, right, and Anant Jeet Singh Naruka compete in the Skeet Mixed Team qualification during the 20th Asian Games, in Nagoya, Japan. (PTI Photo/Atul Yadav)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Anant Jeet Singh Naruka and Parinaaz Dhaliwal added another medal to India’s shooting haul at the Asian Games 2026, winning bronze in the mixed skeet team event at the Aichi-Nagoya Games on Thursday.The Indian pair finished third in the final with 44 hits, behind China, who won gold with 52, and the Republic of Korea, who took silver with 51.India were locked on 44 with Korea after six series in the medal round. However, with the two teams tied, the qualification ranking came into play. Korea had entered the final in the higher qualifying position and therefore retained their place in the gold-medal contest, while India were eliminated and secured bronze. India's progression in the final was 7, 14, 21, 29, 36 and 44 across the six series.China eventually finished on 52 after seven series, with Korea ending on 51. India had completed six series at 44, while Qatar were eliminated earlier and finished fourth on 18.Naruka and Parinaaz had entered the medal round after finishing fourth in qualification with 138 points from 150 targets. Qatar had topped the qualification standings with 145, followed by South Korea on 143 and China on 140.The Indian pair had shot a series of 44, 47 and 47 to make the top four.The bronze also means both shooters leave the Asian Games with two medals each.Naruka had earlier helped India win bronze in the men’s skeet team event, alongside veteran Mairaj Ahmad Khan and Bhavtegh Singh Gill. Naruka had also finished fourth in the individual event.Parinaaz, meanwhile, was part of the Indian women’s skeet team that won bronze on Wednesday along with Raiza Dhillon and Maheshwari Chauhan. Their combined score of 331 gave India its first-ever Asian Games medal in the women’s skeet team event. China won gold while Kazakhstan took silver.The mixed skeet medal takes India’s skeet haul at Aichi-Nagoya to three medals, following the two team bronzes won on Wednesday.India have built on their two-medal haul from the 2022 Asian Games, where Anant Jeet Singh Naruka won silver in the individual event and was part of the men’s team that claimed bronze.The women’s skeet bronze in Aichi-Nagoya is also a landmark result, marking India’s first Asian Games medal in women’s skeet. With three medals across the men’s, women’s and mixed team events, this is India’s best-ever showing in skeet at the Asian Games.
Article Summary: Anant Jeet Singh Naruka and Parinaaz Dhaliwal won bronze in the mixed skeet team event at the Aichi-Nagoya Games on Thursday. The Indian pair finished third in the final with 44 hits, behind China, who won gold with 52, and the Republic of Korea, who took silver with 51. Naruka had earlier helped India win Bronze in the men’s skeetTeam event, alongside veteran Mairaj Ahmad Khan and Bhavtegh Singh Gill. Parinaz was part of the Indian women’Skeet team that won bronze on Wednesday

Article Title: Roshibina Devi wins silver, falls short against China's Zhang Xiaoyu in Asian Games final
Article Text:
India's Naorem Roshibina Devi (PTI Photo)

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Indian wushu player Naorem Roshibina Devi secured her second consecutive Asian Games silver medal after losing the women's sanda 60kg final 0-2 to China's Zhang Xiaoyu at Aichi-Nagoya on Thursday.Zhang dominated the title clash, winning both rounds 5-0 to take the gold medal.Roshibina has now become the first Indian woman to win three consecutive medals in wushu at the Asian Games. She won bronze in 2018 before claiming silver in 2022 and 2026.The Indian, who had also won silver at the 2022 Hangzhou Asian Games, once again fell short against Chinese opposition in the final. She had lost the Hangzhou final to China's Xiaowei Wu.Roshibina enjoyed an impressive campaign in Japan, with her run including a victory over Vietnam's 2023 world champion Nguyen Thi Thu Thuy. She had booked her place in the final after defeating Indonesia's Thania Kusumaningtyas 2-0 in the semi-final on Wednesday.Roshibina's silver is India's 14th medal at the ongoing Asian Games, taking the tally to one gold, six silver and seven bronze medals.Earlier on Thursday, Satnam Singh and Salman Khan won bronze in the men's double sculls final.The Indian pair clocked 6:13.25 to finish third, 3.48 seconds behind China's gold medallists Yi Xudi and Nie Yide and 2.76 seconds behind silver medallists Mekhrojbek Mamatkulov and Pavel Sorin.Satnam and Salman held second position at the 500m, 1000m and 1500m marks but dropped away towards the finish. They were at one stage just half a second behind the Chinese pair.In the men's singles sculls, Balraj Panwar finished fourth after missing out on a medal.Balraj remained second at the 500m, 1000m and 1500m marks before being overtaken by Uzbekistan's Shakhboz Kholmurzaev and Japan's Tatsuya Sakurama in the final 500m.He had a five-second advantage over Sakurama heading into the final stretch but eventually finished eight seconds behind the Japanese rower. Balraj clocked 6:54.80, finishing 15 seconds behind gold medallist Zhiwei Deng of China.
Article Summary: Roshibina becomes first Indian woman to win three consecutive medals in wushu at the Asian Games. Satnam Singh and Salman Khan won bronze in the men's double sculls final. Balraj Panwar finished fourth after missing out on a medal.

Article Title: Satnam-Salman win bronze in men’s double sculls as India add another Asian Games medal
Article Text:
Satnam-Salman win rowing bronze

Satnam Singh and Salman Khan secured a bronze medal for India at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games after finishing third in the men’s double sculls final on Thursday.The Indian pair clocked 6:13.25, with China’s Yi Xudi and Nie Yide taking gold and Uzbekistan’s Mekhrojbek Mamatkulov and Pavel Sorin claiming silver.Satnam and Salman stayed in second place at the 500m, 1000m and 1500m marks and at one stage were just half a second behind the Chinese pair. However, they slipped back in the final stretch to settle for bronze.The Indians finished 3.48 seconds behind the gold medallists and 2.76 seconds behind the silver medallists.In the men’s singles sculls final, Balraj Panwar missed out on a medal after finishing fourth.Balraj held second position at the 500m, 1000m and 1500m marks and entered the final 500m with a five-second advantage over Japan’s Tatsuya Sakurama. However, he was overtaken by Sakurama and Uzbekistan’s Shakhboz Kholmurzaev in the closing stages.Balraj clocked 6:54.80, finishing eight seconds behind Sakurama and 15 seconds behind gold medallist Zhiwei Deng of China.Indian wushu player Naorem Roshibina Devi also settled for silver after losing the women’s sanda 60kg final 0-2 to China’s Zhang Xiaoyu. Zhang won both rounds 5-0 to claim the gold medal. Roshibina has now won silver medals at two consecutive Asian Games, having also lost the 2022 Hangzhou Games final to China’s Xiaowei Wu.Roshibina’s silver took India’s overall medal tally at the ongoing Games to 14, comprising one gold, six silvers and seven bronzes.
Article Summary: Satnam Singh and Salman Khan secured a bronze medal for India at the Aichi- Nagoya Asian Games. The Indian pair clocked 6:13.25, with China’s Yi Xudi and Nie Yide taking gold and Uzbekistan’S Mekhrojbek Mamatkulov and Pavel Sorin claiming silver.

Article Title: Two bronzes amid the gloom: Indian shooters sign off from Asian Games
Article Text:
Nagoya: From left, India's Raiza Dhillon, Maheshwari Chauhan and Parinaaz Dhaliwal pose for photographs after winning bronze in the Skeet Women Team Final event

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Nagoya: The grey cloud cover and steady drizzle at the Aichi Prefectural General Shooting Gallery on Wednesday seemed symbolic of the Indian shooters’ almost damp outing.With six medals up for grabs, India returned with two bronze.Much was expected of the proven women’s air pistol trio of Manu Bhaker Esha Singh and Suruchi Inder Singh. Instead, they finished fourth, nowhere near the silver India won in the event at the 2023 Asian Games.Amid the gloom, however, another group of Indian women shooters added some colour, winning a landmark bronze in the women’s skeet team event.Maheshwari Chauhan, Raiza Dhillon and Parinaaz Dhaliwal combined for 331 points to finish behind China (357) and Kazakhstan (336), earning India its first medal in the women’s skeet team event.Maheshwari, however, was left wanting more.“I’m a little disappointed about it not being a better colour, but it’s better to have finished on the podium,” said the Olympian.Raiza narrowly missed out on an individual medal, finishing fourth.The men’s skeet team also signed off with bronze. Anantjeet Singh Naruka, who finished fourth in the individual event, veteran Mairaj Ahmad Khan and Bhavtegh Singh Gill combined for 346 points.Qatar (352) took gold and Kuwait (348) silver.For Gill, the medal offered relief after a slow start to the competition.“Going home without a medal would have been a little disappointing. So I’m glad we pulled ourselves together on the last day and were able to get the score which we needed,” said the 23-year-old.“It was a tie in the end, but luckily our last one was better than Kazakhstan’s, so we were able to edge them out,” he added.In the much-vaunted 10m pistol, India and Vietnam finished level on 1719 points, but the Vietnamese climbed onto the podium on the inner-10 count. They had 46 shots closest to the centre, compared to India’s 44.India’s 1719-44x was spearheaded by Manu’s 579-20x, which had earned her third place in qualification for the individual final.Esha, the silver medallist from the previous edition, finished 15th with 572-12x, while Suruchi was further down the order with 568-12x (26th place).Manu, who had qualified third, could not raise her game in the individual final either, finishing fifth.
Article Summary: India return with two bronze medals at the 2023 Asian Games in Nagoya. The women's air pistol trio of Manu Bhaker Esha Singh and Suruchi Inder Singh finished fourth. The men's skeet team also signed off with bronze.

Article Title: ‘I will not stop’: Mairaj Ahmad Khan finally wins Asian Games medal after 20 years
Article Text:
Nagoya: From left, India's Mairaj Ahmad Khan, Anantjeet Singh Naruka and Anantjeet Singh Naruka pose for photographs after winning bronze in the Skeet Men Team Final event

Lucknow: Mairaj Ahmad Khan played a key role in India’s podium finish in the men’s skeet team event, which won bronze at the Asian Games on Wednesday.Mairaj, who had previously competed at the Asian Games in 2006, 2010, 2014 and 2026, finally earned a medal at the continental event after 20 years of effort.The 51-year-old from Khurja, Uttar Pradesh, was typically gung-ho after the feat.“Main rukne wala nahin (I will not stop), main haar nahin manunga (I will not give up),” Mairaj told TOI from Japan.“Age does not matter, and I am physically and mentally fit. My main target is the World Championship because it is very important, as it serves as a qualification event for the Los Angeles Olympics. My real goal is the LA Olympics 2028,” he said.Mairaj credited India’s medal-winning effort to team spirit and communication, while praising his younger teammates.
Article Summary: Mairaj Ahmad Khan played a key role in India’s podium finish. The 51-year-old had previously competed at the Asian Games in 2006, 2010, 2014 and 2026. He finally earned a medal at the continental event after 20 years of effort.

Article Title: Juggling Chess Olympiad prep and a commentary gig in India: The other side of USA's only female GM Irina Krush
Article Text:
The other side of America's only grandmaster Irina Krush

Irina Krush (Photo by Photo by Lennart Ootes)

NEW DELHI: For most of its history, American women’s chess had a very simple relationship with the Olympiad podium. It did not have one. Not once, in over four decades of trying, had the United States women’s team finished among the medals at chess’s biennial team championship.Then, in 2002, Susan Polgar switched her allegiance from Hungary to the United States. Two years later, after stepping away from top-level competition to raise her two sons, she sat down on Board 1 in Calvià, Mallorca, and dragged a young, unheralded American team to silver, second only to China and ahead of a Russian juggernaut that had ruled women’s chess for a generation.It was the first medal of any colour the country had ever won in the women’s category.Bronze followed in Dresden four years later, in 2008. And then, after a wait of 16 years that swallowed many careers, bronze again, this time in Budapest, at a tournament where India finally broke through for gold. Three medals across two decades somehow represented three different eras of American chess.The one name, however, that appears on the scoresheet every single time is that of Irina Krush, the first, and to this day the only, woman to earn the Grandmaster (GM) title while playing for the United States.“I was sort of the main player of my generation,” Krush, who is currently playing in her record-extending 13th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, said with a small, knowing smile during an exclusive interaction with TimesofIndia.com.The story does not begin in America. Krush was born in Odesa, in what was then Soviet Ukraine, and arrived in Brooklyn with her parents when she was five years old. Her father, an amateur player of real quality, taught her the moves.Her first tournament against adults followed when she was six, at the Manhattan Chess Club. She made her first appearance for the United States at the World Youth Championship in Poland at seven. By 11, she was already competing in the US Women’s Championship.At 14, in 1998, she won it. Still, almost three decades on, she remains the youngest champion in the event’s history.Krush’s association with India is a long one too. She fondly recalls playing against a young chess prodigy, Koneru Humpy. In the last few years, her association with India has also included a new part of her profession in chess broadcasting and commentary at the Global Chess League (GCL), a league she participated in during its inaugural 2023 season in Dubai, on a roster built around Magnus Carlsen.“It was a chance to play in the same team as Magnus, and it was like a very special opportunity,” Krush added. “I definitely thought that was like a highlight of my chess career.”But a highlight, in her telling, was never the same thing as a comfortable one. “It’s also — you feel the pressure, right? Because you don’t want to look like the fool on the team with Magnus,” she chuckled. “There are two sides to that coin. But overall, it was a very good experience.”She has not played in the league since. What she has done, for the next two seasons, is commentate on it, first in Mumbai and, more recently, in Bengaluru, watching from the other side of the glass.This time, Krush arrived in India with the 46th Chess Olympiad bearing down on her. For more than two decades, the tournament has been the anchor of her competitive identity, and this year, the games in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, were set to begin just two days after her India schedule wrapped up.The commentary booth, for all it has given her, though, has eaten directly into the time she would otherwise have spent getting ready for it.Asked plainly whether she had found any window to play or prepare between broadcasts, she replied: “So far, no. It’s only been a few days, but it’s been so busy. Today, we were asked to appear at the golf thing. So I had to get up at 7:45 in the morning, go to that. Then I had another nap, and then I just had to go here. So it’s a long day. And honestly, I have not had a chance to do much chess for myself at all.”It is a trade she has made with her eyes open, not a complaint dressed up as one. She had spent the months before India trying to bank the form the broadcast schedule was about to interrupt.“I’ve spent the summer playing tournaments, and I just finished a tournament the day before I came here,” she told this website. “There’s definitely been an attempt to try to get myself into good playing condition.”And on the final day, when the commentators were felicitated on the main stage for being the voice of the league, Krush, who became a grandmaster in 2013, barely lingered after the ceremony. She left the arena almost immediately, the next challenge, the Samarkand Olympiad, already waiting.For someone who has spent much of her career playing chess at the highest level, commentary came without formal preparation.“I never did anything special. I don’t have any training in commentary,” she said. “But, you know, it comes kind of naturally for me to talk about chess. It’s something that’s very easy to talk about and get excited about. I like to watch chess.”Her preparation for the booth is less about learning how to commentate and more about doing what she has always done with chess: looking closely at the players and their games.“You definitely try to do some preparation,” she said. “So, you have ways to fill up, you know, give some context for what’s happening. How are the players doing? So, it just requires a little bit of research, you know, to come up with those nuggets that people will find interesting.”But even that preparation changes as a tournament begins to take shape. “At the beginning, you’re doing more general research,” she further noted. “And after the players have started playing against each other, then you’re already more interested in what’s happening in this tournament. What’s the recent results? Not like what happened one year ago in their other matchups.”“As the tournament continues, you start focussing more. What happened in the first half? How do they do again? How are they overall doing in the tournament?” Krush continued.“The tournament itself becomes more of a focus than their history before. Because it’s all now about, like, now you’ve already seen their recent form. So, you focus more on that. Looking at the games is the best part.”The difficulty comes when the chess stops. “The only challenge is, like, maybe sometimes you gotta fill up the time,” she admitted. “You know, the games are over. For me, it’s like, okay, just commenting on the things that are not as exciting for me. You know, just figuring out what to say.“But when we’re on the chess, it’s the easiest.”The United States are among the leading teams at the Women’s Chess Olympiad, with a squad featuring Carissa Yip, Alice Lee, Rose Atwell and Tatev Abrahamyan, alongside the most experienced Irina Krush.“It’s like a very nice mix of the young players who are really kind of, they’re not even at their peak yet necessarily, but they’re definitely rising,” Krush said. “And then, okay, like there’s me and Tatev, and we kind of bring a lot of experience to the team. Playing for like 20 years or more for the Olympiad.”That depth, the 42-year-old says, is the product of a sport that barely resembles the one she came up in.“It’s much more competitive (now). There’s more incentive to play chess, more opportunities to play,” the eight-time US women’s champion shared. “We didn’t have the kinds of prizes we have at the US championships 25 years ago. We didn’t have an American Cup. We didn’t have a Cairns Cup. We didn’t have the Cairns Queen chess award for the next woman who’s gonna become a grandmaster in America.”The dividend, she adds, is visible in the players coming up behind her now.“A whole generation of strong girls coming up, with Carissa and Alice being kind of the main ones, but also other young girls who are close to 2400 as well,” Krush acknowledged.In Uzbekistan, the US women’s team made a dream start, but its campaign soon lost momentum. A draw against Uzbekistan was followed by a defeat to India, leaving Krush’s team in 14th place in the rankings heading into the rest day.For someone who has now spent two seasons narrating other people’s games for a living, Krush is unsentimental about what the job actually requires.Asked what advice she would give someone hoping to follow her into a commentary booth, she does not reach for a formula.ALSO READ: From uplifting heartbroken team to calling out Chess Olympiad hotel mess: Srinath is India's man to count on “Honestly, there’s just a lot of people who are doing it these days, and everyone brings their own special thing to it, right? So you have different styles. You could be like a top GM and then just start doing commentary. You could be like a different level enthusiast and do commentary,” she concluded, while instinctively running her tongue once again along the outside of her gum. “So I really don’t have any advice except I feel like anyone who loves chess and is pretty good at it can do it. ”
Article Summary: Irina Krush is the only woman to earn the Grandmaster title while playing for the United States. She is currently playing in her record-extending 13th Chess Olympiad in Samarkand, Uzbekistan. Krush was born in Odesa, in what was then Soviet Ukraine, and arrived in Brooklyn with her parents when she was five.

Article Title: Asian Games hockey: Deepika's nine-goal show powers India to 20-1 win over Thailand

NEW DELHI: Deepika produced a stunning nine-goal show as India continued their dominant run in women's hockey at the 2026 Asian Games, thrashing Thailand 20-1 in their Pool B match at the Gifu Prefectural Green Stadium on Wednesday.The forward and drag-flick specialist converted all nine of her goals from penalty corners as India registered their third straight victory of the competition.The win kept the Sjoerd Marijne-coached side at the top of the Pool B standings.Deepika was the star of the match, scoring nine times in a remarkable individual performance.All nine goals came from penalty corners, with Deepika repeatedly finding a way past the Thailand defence as India dominated the contest.Navneet Kaur added four goals, while Rutuja Pisal completed her hat-trick.Neha, Lalremsiami, Sakshi Rana and captain Salima Tete also found the net as India maintained pressure throughout the match.Thailand managed to avoid a clean sheet only late in the fourth quarter.Supansa Samanso scored Thailand's only goal with a drag-flick from a penalty corner. Her effort took a slight deflection before finding its way into the Indian goal.It was the only time Thailand managed to beat the Indian defence.India had opened their campaign with a 19-0 win over Uzbekistan before following it up with a 17-1 victory over Indonesia.Deepika had also scored a hat-trick against Indonesia, while Rutuja and Navneet also hit three goals each in that match.Sunelita Toppo, Lalremsiami and Sakshi scored two goals apiece, while Ishika and Salima also found the target.India took some time to settle against Indonesia, but Deepika broke the deadlock in the eighth minute after India earned four penalty corners in quick succession.Against Thailand, Deepika once again showed why she is such an important part of India's penalty-corner attack.India will next face Japan on Friday as they look to strengthen their position ahead of the knockout stages.The Indian team are looking to improve on their bronze-medal finish at the 2023 Hangzhou Asian Games They are also chasing their first Asian Games gold in women's hockey since 1982, when India won the inaugural women's hockey title at the Games on home soil.With three straight wins and 56 goals in their opening matches, India have made a strong start to their Pool B campaign.And after Deepika's nine-goal performance against Thailand, India's attacking threat looks even stronger heading into the next stage of the competition.
Article Summary: Deepika scores nine goals as India thrash Thailand 20-1 in 2026 Asian Games. Navneet Kaur added four goals, while Rutuja Pisal completed her hat-trick. Neha, Lalremsiami, Sakshi Rana and captain Salima Tete also scored.

Article Title: 'The night I could not sleep': Gautam Gambhir opens up on 'toughest decision' to drop Sanju Samson for Vaibhav Sooryavanshi
Article Text:
vaibhav sooryavanshi, gautam gambhir, sanju samson

India head coach Gautam Gambhir has revealed the emotional difficulty behind one of his biggest selection calls in T20Is, admitting that dropping Sanju Samson during the England series left him unable to sleep.Samson, who was named Player of the Tournament during India's T20 World Cup triumph earlier this year, was left out after the first match of the five-game series in England in July. India had lost that opening T20I, with teenage sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi coming into the XI for his T20I debut in Manchester.Gambhir said the decision weighed heavily on him, particularly because Samson had played such an important role in India's World Cup success. Speaking to JioStar ahead of India's home season against the West Indies, the India coach revealed just how difficult the call was."In two years of my journey, that was the only night I could not sleep and I told this to Sanju because I knew that it was probably the toughest decision in my coaching tenure in a T20 format because someone who was player of the tournament, and then you have to leave him out after three or four games.And the reason was probably Vaibhav was in that kind of form as well, and we had to win the series.“Because ultimately you are there and when you are playing for India, or when you are coaching India, you want to win each and every series possible. I had a very, very honest conversation with him and I told him that that is one of the reasons why, because Vaibhav was in that kind of form, and we needed someone to score runs at the top, we needed that little bit of a platform at the top as well. And he was fine with it. And that's a conversation which me and Sanju had, and he took it in good spirits," said Gambhir.The call was eventually reversed when India returned home for their three-match T20I series against Afghanistan. Samson came back into the side at Sooryavanshi's expense and went on to hit back-to-back fifties as India completed a 3-0 series sweep.Gambhir also used the episode to explain why even a player in exceptional form cannot automatically expect a place in India's playing XI."I know, it is (tough). But then, I made him understand that I know you're in good form, but sometimes with the players who have done well for a long time, you will have to wait for your opportunity.“There’s one more thing - social media or outside noise doesn't decide the playing eleven. Playing eleven who, in that dressing room, or who the coach and captain feel can win us the match, or what is the best playing eleven, and who have done well for such a long time because if Vaibhav plays today, then it's going to be a tough conversation between me and whoever we leave out, whether it's Abhishek or Sanju.“So we can't suddenly ignore that a combination that has created such an impact over the last one and a half or two years, that after three or four failures we drop them and play a young player who is very talented, who is also in very good form.“So sometimes you will have to wait for your opportunity and we still want to create that security in that dressing room. Because it is very easy for me to take popular decisions, but it is probably the toughest thing for me to take the right decisions and we've taken the right decision of continuing with Sanju and Abhishek," he explained.Sooryavanshi's emergence has nevertheless added another dimension to India's T20I selection puzzle. The teenager made his international debut in Manchester, but Gambhir stressed that India's established combination cannot be discarded simply because a young player is performing well.For the India coach, maintaining continuity remains particularly important given the team's recent success. Gambhir pointed to the short turnaround between India's World Cup triumphs while arguing against overreacting to isolated setbacks."For two years, imagine, you imagine we won the World Cup - which team in the history of sport has gone undefeated from one World Cup to the other and gone on to win the World Cup?“It didn't take these guys 17 years to win the second World Cup. It took these guys only 17 months to win the third World Cup. Suddenly one bad series or three bad games here and there does not make them a bad player or does not make us a bad side. So it was very important for us to have that continuity."
Article Summary: Gautam Gambhir admits dropping Sanju Samson during the England series left him unable to sleep. Samson was named Player of the Tournament during India's T20 World Cup triumph earlier this year. India coach also used the episode to explain why even a player in exceptional form cannot automatically expect a place in India's playing XI.

England Test captain Joe Root's younger brother, Billy Root, has announced his retirement from professional cricket at the age of 34.Root is one of three Glamorgan batters whose playing careers will end this week, along with Chris Cooke and Colin Ingram. He had a limited role in his final season, playing only two County Championship matches and captaining Glamorgan's second XI.Announcing his retirement on social media, Root said it was "time for the next chapter" in his life."It has been an absolute privilege to represent two great clubs and to share in the success of four trophy wins," Root said. "I feel incredibly lucky to have had the opportunity to make a career out of something I have loved since I was a kid."There have been plenty of ups and downs over the last 14 years, but I wouldn't change a thing. I'll always be incredibly grateful for the journey, the people l've shared it with and the opportunity to live out a childhood dream. Thank you to everyone who has played a part."Root began his professional career with Nottinghamshire after studying at Leeds Beckett University. He was part of the Nottinghamshire squad that won the white-ball double in 2017.He moved to Glamorgan in 2019 and was part of the team that won two One-Day Cup titles. He also played a role in the club's promotion to Division One of the County Championship last summer.Root grew up playing cricket with his older brother Joe at Sheffield Collegiate CC. The brothers briefly shared the field during a Test at Lord's in 2013, when Billy, then with MCC Young Cricketers, was named as England's 12th man.Glamorgan director of cricket Mark Wallace paid tribute to Root's contribution to the club."Billy has been a hugely important part of Glamorgan over the last seven seasons. South Africa captain Temba Bavuma said his team will need to make the most of its depleted fast bowling attack when they host Australia in a three-match ODI series starting in Durban on Thursday.South Africa are without Kagiso Rabada , Lungi Ngidi, Kwena Maphaka and Ottneil Baartman, who have been ruled out with hamstring injuries. Nandre Burger is also unavailable because of a back injury.Bavuma said having a strong group of fast bowlers for visiting teams to face is part of South African cricket's "DNA", but the injuries have forced the team to look beyond its usual options for the series.Lizaad Williams, the Jansen twins Marco and Duan, Gerald Coetzee, Corbin Bosch and Nqobani Mokoena have played only 72 ODIs between them."I think we're going to have to make the most of the bowling resources that we have from the seam department. There are options there. I think it's just how smartly we approach managing the loads of our fast bowlers," Bavuma told reporters on Wednesday, as quoted by news agency Reuters."We want teams, when they come here, to know that they're going to have to deal with our fast bowlers. That's part of our DNA."South Africa have played only three ODIs in 2026. They won all three against Namibia in a series earlier this month with a depleted squad.With South Africa set to host the 2027 World Cup next year, the current season is an important one for the team in the 50-over format."It's been a while since this ODI team has come together," Bavuma said. "I think there's a strong desire to look after our ODI record of late and ensure that we're putting our best foot forward out there on the field."Bavuma said the team already has an idea of the core group it wants for the World Cup and is unlikely to make major changes."From a team perspective, we generally know who those core players are (for the World Cup). I don't think we will move away too much from that," he added.There will be new players coming into the squad, but Bavuma said the three-match series against England in January 2027 could give a clearer picture of the team South Africa expect to take into the World Cup."We'll see new faces coming in, but probably that England series (in January 2027) will be closer to what we think we will have for the World Cup."

But you can look at my average in domestic cricket, whether it’s in one-dayers or four-day matches. I have a dream of playing Test cricket for India as well.“So, people shouldn’t view me as a single-format player. I can play all three formats, and I do play all three formats in domestic cricket. But for India, I play only one format at the moment.”Rinku also spoke about his development as a leader and said he is still learning from experienced captains in domestic and franchise cricket.“I’m still growing as far as captaincy is concerned. I was captaining in the UP League, and I became champion with my team. Last season, I was the vice-captain in the IPL.“So, I’m learning the ropes of captaincy, a bit from Ajju bhai (Ajinkya Rahane) at KKR and from many others. I played a lot with Surya bhai, so I kept observing him in the Indian team for two years and watching how he leads. I’m working on my leadership skills, and hopefully, something good is in store for me in captaincy.”Rinku also reflected on his journey from humble beginnings to becoming an India cricketer.He said looking back at his past keeps him grounded.“When I look back at where I began, I didn’t have much, and now I’ve reached here. That keeps running through my mind, the fact that there was a time when I had nothing, no money.“Whenever I do something good, I think back to where I was and how far I have come from there. It’s all God’s blessing. So, I keep looking back at how far I have come,” he concluded.
Article Summary: Rinku Singh hopes Virat Kohli and Rohit Sharma feature in the 2027 ODI World Cup. The middle-order batter also wants to move beyond the perception of being a single-format player and earn a Test cap for India. Rinku has played two ODIs and 48 T20Is so far.

Article Title: ‘We want to see him under pressure’: New Zealand coach lays down challenge for Vaibhav Sooryavanshi
Article Text:
Vaibhav Sooryavanshi

New Zealand head coach Rob Walter is keen to see how India’s teenage batting sensation Vaibhav Sooryavanshi handles the challenge of pace and bounce when the two sides meet in the upcoming T20I series.Sooryavanshi has already made a name for himself with explosive performances in the IPL in 2025 and 2026, as well as at this year’s U19 World Cup. Those displays earned him his T20I debut against England in July.The teenager was part of India’s squad for the 3-0 T20I series win over Afghanistan and the narrow two-run victory over Japan in Sano, but did not feature in the playing eleven.Walter said he would be particularly interested in watching Sooryavanshi bat on the seam-friendly, bouncy New Zealand surfaces and also see how he responds if put under pressure.“Yes, I'd love to see him on some pace in bouncy wickets and see how different that looks. But he's an exciting player. You've seen him dominate against the world's best bowlers in the IPL. I think the challenge is always to see how that translates to different conditions and also how do we bowl to him in our conditions.“Again, secretly as a coach, you always want to see your players under a little bit of pressure and how we respond to that.So looking forward to it, if that is the case. If he's not here, they do have a lot of very good players other than him,” Walter told reporters on Wednesday.The New Zealand coach was also asked about the controversial wide call during India’s recent one-off T20I against Japan, which sparked considerable debate.Walter made it clear that he had not followed the match closely and had little interest in getting drawn into the controversy.“A very short segment (I watched). I saw there was some controversy around the wide ruling. But no, I didn't watch a hell of a lot of it, to be fair. The lesser the better, I think.”The upcoming series will also bring New Zealand back together for their first T20I engagement as a collective since the T20 World Cup final in Ahmedabad, where they suffered a heavy defeat to India.Walter acknowledged that losing a final naturally leaves a mark, but insisted the Black Caps' motivation for the home series is not centred on revenge.“I suppose it is there. No one likes to lose a final. I've done it twice, so I know all about it. But I think what comes first is representing the Black Caps and New Zealand well. So you've got a group of players who are always trying to do that first. Of course, if you manage to get a couple of victories at home, that would be great.“But taking care of the little steps in between now and then is the most important part. Being excited about representing again - it's been a while for some of the guys. Obviously it's the first time as a collective since the World Cup, with the majority of the squad that was in the World Cup to run out together.“So there's always something in it. It's not our major focal point, certainly not the things we speak about the most. Most importantly, we want to play good cricket and represent well,” he explained.
Article Summary: Vaibhav Sooryavanshi made his T20I debut against England in July. The teenager has already made a name for himself with explosive performances in the IPL in 2025 and 2026, as well as at this year’s U19 World Cup. New Zealand head coach Rob Walter is keen to see how the teenager handles pace and bounce.
